levels.note: Tiny crystals seen under a microscope

explain.say: Polish a piece of steel, etch it with acid and look under a microscope: it is a patchwork of tiny crystals called grains. Zoom further and every grain is atoms stacked in a perfect repeating pattern. Look at the zoom: from a bracket you can hold down to a single atom.

draw.text: Unit cell: the smallest box that repeats to build the crystal

explain.say: Most metals use one of three patterns. Body-centred cubic, BCC, has an atom at each corner of a cube and one in the middle. Face-centred cubic, FCC, has an atom at each corner and one in the centre of each face. Hexagonal close-packed, HCP, stacks layers like oranges on a market stall. See the groups?

draw.text: BCC: 2 atoms per cell; FCC: 4 atoms per cell

explain.say: How tightly do they pack? The atomic packing factor is the volume of atoms over the volume of the cell. In FCC the atoms touch along the face diagonal, so the cube side is 2 root 2 times the atom radius. Four atoms fill 74 percent of the box. BCC fills only 68 percent. Which do you think is denser packed, FCC or HCP?

They tie: both are 74 percent, the tightest packing possible for equal spheres. Structure decides behaviour. FCC metals like aluminium and copper have many close-packed planes that slide easily, so they bend without cracking, even when very cold. HCP metals like magnesium have fewer slip planes and are less ductile at room temperature.

Fantastic. And iron changes its mind! Below 912 degrees it is BCC; above, it turns FCC. That switch is the secret behind hardening steel, the next lesson. Exam tip: for aluminium, cube side 0.405 nanometres gives an atomic radius of 0.143. Challenge: why do BCC steels turn brittle in Arctic cold?

faq.a: The smallest group of atoms that, repeated in three dimensions, builds the whole crystal. Metals mostly use cubic or hexagonal unit cells.

faq.q: What is the difference between BCC and FCC?
faq.a: BCC has atoms at the cube corners plus one at the centre, packing 68 percent of space. FCC has atoms at the corners and face centres, packing 74 percent, with more close-packed slip planes, so FCC metals are usually more ductile.

faq.q: Why is aluminium more ductile than iron at room temperature?
faq.a: Aluminium is FCC, with many close-packed planes that slip easily, so it stays ductile even at low temperatures. Iron at room temperature is BCC, which is strong but can turn brittle when very cold.
HCP stacks close-packed layers in an ABAB pattern. It packs 74 percent of space like FCC but has fewer easy slip systems, so metals like magnesium and zinc are less ductile at room temperature.

faq.q: Why does iron change crystal structure?
faq.a: Iron is an allotropic metal: it is BCC below 912 degrees, FCC between 912 and 1394, and BCC again until it melts. The FCC form can dissolve much more carbon, which makes heat treatment of steel possible.

facts: FCC and HCP both have an atomic packing factor of 0.74; BCC has 0.68.
Pure iron changes from BCC to FCC at 912 °C.
